Policymakers take on energy shock, rising debt at IMF-World Bank meetings
item.description:
Finance ministers and central bankers meet in Bangkok this week for the annual gatherings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, with the global economy buffeted between the US-Iran war's energy shock, rising debt pressures and the AI boom.

The meetings run from Monday through Saturday in the Thai capital, and will see policymakers tackle some stark choices, with the IMF calling on governments to rein in spending even as vulnerable citizens'' needs may be growing in the face of surging inflation and climate risks.

The week will see a combination of high-level closed-door meetings, public events and policy announcements from the world's top economic officials.
On Tuesday, the IMF will unveil its global economic forecast, along with detailed regional outlooks through the week, as policymakers set about tackling the challenges darkening the economic horizon.

In Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva highlighted how the world economy was being pulled in opposite directions by the negative energy supply shock caused by the US war on Iran and the positive demand shock of the artificial intelligence technology boom.

"That shift into higher gear (from AI) is what is keeping the world economy growing at three percent," she told an event on the first day of the meetings, adding the growth was "despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock."

At a press briefing, World Bank President Ajay Banga told AFP his message to developing countries on AI was to focus on building "small AI" applications, rather than trying to compete on capital-intensive models.

"Don't try and compete with America and China on frontier models and large data centres," he said. "You don''t have the computing power. You don't have the electricity. You don''t have the people."

Banga said AI-powered applications could run on less powerful smartphones and be used in healthcare, education, agriculture and other fields that are development priorities for low-income countries.

''Perfect storm''

Chief among concerns in Bangkok will be the economic fallout of the US war on Iran, which has seen energy prices skyrocket as Tehran''s retaliatory action has targeted Washington''s Gulf allies and curtailed global oil and gas supplies.

The IMF has warned that the effects of the shock have been unequal, with developing countries reliant on imported energy hit the hardest.
Despite the crisis, the Fund has called on countries to curb spending on subsidies and instead build their fiscal buffers after years of shocks since the pandemic.

Critics say that approach is just not feasible for low-income countries, and that multilateral lenders need to do more.

"The poorer member states of the IMF and World Bank are in distress from spillovers of the Iran war, rising interest rates in the West, and a climate crisis exacerbated by El Nino," said Kevin P. Gallagher, director of Boston University's Global Development Policy Center.

"The IMF and World Bank are not meeting this moment. They need an ambitious response that provides short-term emergency liquidity alongside longer term financing to make their economic growth paths less vulnerable to these shocks."

And the needs are great, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

The combined shocks "could leave millions more in poverty as developing countries struggle to sustain support for households," the UNDP warned in a report on Sunday.

"We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty," said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.

In the developing world, he added, governments are being forced to make the "impossible" choice between cutting support for their poorest citizens or risking their entire development agenda.

Advanced economies in Europe and the United States have weathered the storm from the rising energy prices better, but have not been immune to surging inflation fuelled by those price increases, which have begun to bleed into other goods.

That inflation has seen central banks around the world raise interest rates in an effort to curb rising prices, tapping the brakes on economic activity.
Still, advanced economies have seen a boom in investment in artificial intelligence technology drive stock markets to new highs and bolster economic growth.

The week will also see several key meetings on the sidelines, including of G20 finance ministers, where spiking bond yields will be high on the agenda.

A notable absence at that meeting will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who will skip due to "domestic engagements", a department official said on Friday.

item.title: Charges brought against 2 former army officers, put on 4-day remand
item.description:
Former two army officers, Lieutenant Colonel (Retd.) Debashish and Lieutenant (Retd.) Kazi Gulshan Ara, have been arrested by the Detective Branch of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP).

Police stated that they were arrested under the Anti-Terrorism Act and Cyber Security Act cases.

According to police, they were arrested late last night during a raid in the capital. The operation was conducted by members of the Pallabi Zonal Team of DMP's Detective Branch. They were apprehended from a house in the Banani DOHS area at around 2: 30 AM.

Pallabi Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Jalal Uddin told Prothom Alo that a DB police inspector has filed a case against the former army officers under the Anti-Terrorism Act and Cyber Security Act.

The case statement alleges that the arrested former army officers and their associates are involved in anti-government propaganda, fund-raising, and creating and promoting provocative digital content for violence on various social media platforms.

Additionally, they are accused of maintaining contact with former army chief General (Retd.) Aziz Ahmed and former Home Minister and top fugitive leaders through a platform named 'Unity Care Public Parliament' and are involved in conspiracies against the state.

The statement further claims that content was being created with the intent to incite violence and instability through a page called ''KalAjkal. com''. They are also accused of conducting and promoting various anti-state activities using social media.

According to the police's statement, they are accused of illegal financing with the intention of operating banned organisational activities and involvement in offences under various clauses of the Anti-Terrorism Act and Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025. The statement mentions that since 5 August 2024, they have been conspiring against the government and Bangladesh alongside their associates and conducting slanderous propaganda.

Moreover, Lieutenant (Retd.) Kazi Gulshan Ara is accused of publicly expressing solidarity and loyalty to the then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina with more than one and a half hundred retired army officers before the election on 27 November 2018. The statement also includes accusations of forming a committee named Bangladesh Army Council and spreading hatred among various classes and professions through the organisation.

Four-day remand granted

The court has granted a four-day remand for questioning the former army officers in this case. Dhaka's Metropolitan Magistrate Didarul Alam gave this order on Monday evening after a hearing. The state's lawyer Harun Or Rashid confirmed this information to Prothom Alo.

Before this, the investigation officer of the case, Inspector Sheikh Bashir Ahmed of DB's Cyber and Special Crime Division, presented former army officers Debashish and Gulshan Ara in court seeking a seven-day remand.

The remand application stated the necessity to identify and locate other accused individuals, verify the involvement of domestic and foreign individuals, recover digital evidence, search for any other websites or pages operated by the accused, and uncover the main mystery of the incident.

Around 5: 45 PM, defendants Debashish and Gulshan Ara were presented in the dock. The judge appeared shortly thereafter. The investigation officer then presented arguments in favour of the remand application, stating that they participated in WhatsApp meetings with the former Home Minister engaging in various plots to destabilise the country. Additionally, other various incriminating elements were found, prompting the remand request.

During this time, defendant's lawyer Abdullah Al Monsur requested to dismiss the remand application, stating that Lieutenant Colonel (Retd.) Debashish is the second accused in this case and claims against him are unacceptable. He questioned the rationale for the treason charge, stating that his crimes were not articulated in the remand plea.

And Gulshan Ara's lawyer Mohammad Moshiur Rahman argued that the accusation of attempting to destabilise the country by appearing on a talk show lacks substance as there is no mention of any destabilising statements made. The remand plea lacks grounds for the accused to be taken into custody.

Then, the state lawyer Harun Or Rashid argued for the remand, saying, "The accused have maintained regular contact with leaders and activists of the fallen government to destabilise the country. There is contact with local and international spies. We seek a seven-day remand to gather more information about their connections, sabotage activities, and their plans. "
After hearing from both sides, the court granted a four-day remand.

item.title: Durga Puja holidays: Banks, stock markets to remain closed for five consecutive days
item.description:
All scheduled banks in the country will remain closed for three days, from 20 to 22 October, for the upcoming Durga Puja festival. The following two days, Friday and Saturday, are weekly holidays. As a result, banks will remain closed for five consecutive days, from 20 to 24 October.

Bangladesh Bank issued a circular on Sunday announcing the directive. However, banks have been instructed to remain open on weekly holiday, Saturday, 17 October, as on a regular working day.

Durga Puja: Extended holiday gazette issued, what will remain open

Meanwhile, no trading will take place on the country’s two stock exchanges—the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) and the Chittagong Stock Exchange (CSE)—during the bank holidays.

As stock market transactions are linked to banking operations, the stock markets will also remain closed for five consecutive days.

Although banks will remain closed from 20 to 22 October, limited banking services will continue in port and customs areas to keep import and export activities running.

5-day Durga Puja holiday; offices to remain open on preceding Saturday

The Bangladesh Bank circular further states that bank branches and booths in seaports, land ports and airports, including port and customs areas, must maintain limited operations during the Puja holidays to ensure that the country’s import and export trade continues uninterrupted.

Banks will take the necessary measures after consulting local administrations and port or customs authorities.

On 7 October, the Ministry of Public Administration issued a circular declaring holidays from 20 to 22 October for Sharadiya Durga Puja. It stated that all government, semi-government, autonomous, semi-autonomous and private offices would remain open on Saturday, 17 October.

item.title: 51 flights cancelled or suspended from Dhaka, 5,418 passengers affected
item.description:
The suspension of flight operations at various airports in Saudi Arabia has directly affected 51 flights operated by airlines serving Bangladesh through direct and transit routes.

Some flights have been cancelled, while others have been suspended. A total of 5,418 passengers scheduled to travel from Dhaka to various destinations in Saudi Arabia have been affected.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) disclosed the information in a press release on Monday afternoon. The flights were cancelled or suspended between Saturday night and Monday afternoon.

According to CAAB, 12 of the 51 affected flights were direct services to and from Saudi Arabia, while the remaining 39 were transit flights. The direct flights included four operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia and three by Riyadh Air.

Among the transit flights, 16 were operated by IndiGo, three by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, nine by Emirates, five by Qatar Airways and five by flydubai.

According to the latest information from CAAB, the impact of restrictions on operations at Saudi airports is no longer limited to direct flights. Transit flights operated by various international airlines have also been affected, creating uncertainty for passengers' travel plans.

According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, all flights bound for Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled. A Reuters report said the decision followed a major attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital on Saturday.

Reporting the suspension of flights at Riyadh's international airport, Reuters said airport authorities had advised passengers to contact their respective airlines before travelling to the airport and check the latest status of their flights.

US-Bangla cancels all Riyadh flights until 21 October

Private carrier US-Bangla Airlines said in a press release that all its flights on the Dhaka–Riyadh–Dhaka route had been cancelled until 21 October due to the closure of Riyadh airport. The affected flights are BS 381 and BS 382.

The airline said passengers would be informed once a revised flight schedule was finalised.

US-Bangla has requested passengers travelling to Saudi Arabia not to go to the airport for the time being. Passengers have been advised to contact the airline's sales centres or their travel agencies before visiting the airport to obtain updates on flight status, rebooking and other information. The airline apologised for the temporary inconvenience.

Expatriate workers from different parts of Bangladesh arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka to travel to Saudi Arabia but were unable to leave because of flight cancellations and suspensions.

‘If I cannot return now, I will lose my job’

Abul Hossain was scheduled to fly to Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight at 2pm on Monday. He arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka from Senbagh in Noakhali at around 10am to catch the flight, only to learn that it had been cancelled.

Hossain said he had been working in Saudi Arabia for six years and was currently employed as a tile mason in Riyadh. He had returned to Bangladesh on a three-month leave and had booked his return ticket three months in advance in line with his leave schedule.

The cancellation has left him worried about returning to his workplace.

“My leave has ended. If I cannot go back now, I will not be able to keep my job. Everything will become uncertain,” Abul Hossain told Prothom Alo.

Flight information board at the airport

Like Hossain, Md Moslem Talukdar also had his flight cancelled. His flight to Riyadh was scheduled for 12:10pm Bangladesh time. He had been waiting at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport since 10am when he learnt that the flight had been cancelled.

Speaking to Prothom Alo at around 3:30pm, Moslem Talukdar said, “My flight was scheduled for noon, but I could not leave. The airport is shut, and the flight has been cancelled. I am now checking whether I can travel on another flight. Otherwise, I will have to return home.”

He said he was due to join work at a shop in Riyadh.

Between 1pm and 4:30pm on Monday, Prothom Alo spoke to more than 15 passengers who had arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport to travel to Saudi Arabia. Most of them were unaware that their flights had been cancelled, while some were waiting to see whether they could reach their destinations on alternative flights.

item.title: Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.

The airport cancelled 99.7 per cent of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group LHAG.DEhas cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM AIRF.PA has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6 per cnet this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

item.title: Iran says ‘deeply concerned’ over escalation between Houthis, Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Iran said Monday it was “deeply concerned” by escalating attacks between Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, after 14 people died in two days of strikes on Riyadh’s airport.
“We are deeply concerned about the developments taking place in the Arabian Peninsula,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told a weekly press conference, adding that Tehran was ready “to help facilitate dialogue between the parties.”
A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11 others, a day after 13 died in the deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
“We absolutely do not want hostilities and war to continue between two Islamic countries,” Baqaei said, urging the parties to resolve the situation “through dialogue and engagement.”
The Houthis are part of the Iran-backed “Axis of Resistance,” a network of groups opposed to Israel that also includes Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi Shiite armed groups.

item.title: PM seeks Canadian support in energy, agriculture, climate finance
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday sought Canadian support in energy, agriculture and climate finance, while stressing the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of around 1.3 million Rohingyas to Myanmar as the only sustainable solution to the crisis.
He made the call when a Canadian delegation, led by its Secretary of State (International Development) Randeep Sarai, met him at his office at the Secretariat.
The meeting discussed strengthening bilateral relations, expanding economic cooperation and exploring new opportunities for a strategic partnership between Bangladesh and Canada, said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
Other key issues included technical and vocational education, food security, poverty alleviation and renewable energy.
On the Rohingya crisis, Tarique Rahman said Bangladesh is hosting around 1.3 million Rohingyas, putting considerable pressure on the country’s economy and environment while it continues to address its own economic and social challenges.
He said humanitarian assistance for the displaced people remained important, but their safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation is the only sustainable solution to the crisis, which originated in Myanmar and must be resolved there.
Randeep Sarai agreed on the importance of ensuring the peaceful, safe and dignified repatriation of Rohingyas.
The Canadian side expressed interest in cooperating with Bangladesh on energy supplies, particularly oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), saying Canada could be a potential partner in these areas.
Bangladesh said it will consider the proposal positively.
Canada expressed interest in expanding cooperation in technical and vocational education and training (TVET) in Bangladesh.
The two sides also discussed cooperation in establishing nursing training institutions and developing skilled nurses. Canada already has activities in this sector and plans to expand them further, the meeting was told.
The meeting discussed opportunities to strengthen cooperation in the production and supply of agricultural commodities, including pulses and oilseeds.
Canada expressed interest in supporting Bangladesh’s efforts to ensure food security.
The Prime Minister was also briefed on existing programmes being implemented through the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT).
The two sides also discussed Bangladesh’s Farmers’ Card programme, under which the government plans to provide farmers with essential agricultural inputs, including fertiliser and seeds.
Tarique Rahman said the programme will help the government maintain detailed information on farmers, enabling better agricultural planning and more effective delivery of public support.
The meeting discussed how Bangladesh could benefit from Canada’s experience in data management and evidence-based planning in this sector.
Referring to World Bank data, the Prime Minister said integrating multiple food subsidy programmes, improving the aims of existing cash assistance schemes and linking them with the Family Card could help lift an additional 2.85 million people out of poverty.
He stressed the importance of economic self-reliance, saying his government is focusing not only on social protection but also on expanding income and employment opportunities to help people become self-sufficient.
The meeting discussed Bangladesh’s renewable energy initiatives, canal excavation and the programme to plant 250 million trees.
Randeep Sarai said Canada is interested in providing C$13 billion in global climate finance over the next five years, noting that Bangladesh could benefit from the funding.
Canada also expressed interest in supporting feasibility studies for development projects in Bangladesh.
The Canadian secretary of state praised Bangladeshis and people of Bangladeshi origin living in Canada for their initiative, skills and positive outlook.
He also informed the Prime Minister that two people of Bangladeshi origin are serving as members of the Canadian Parliament.
At the end of the meeting, Sarai invited Tarique Rahman to visit Canada.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Education, Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Mahdi Amin, Press Secretary Saleh Shibly and relevant officials attended the meeting.
Canadian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Ajit Singh and senior officials from the Canadian side were also present.

item.title: Saudi crisis exposes Bangladesh’s migrant labour vulnerability
item.description:
Bangladeshi migrant workers in Saudi Arabia are facing a deepening livelihood crisis as missile attacks and flight disruptions compound existing problems of unpaid wages, shrinking employment opportunities and difficulties renewing residency permits, raising concerns over the future of Bangladesh’s largest overseas labour market.
The situation has worsened following the deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, which killed two Bangladeshis and injured 24 others, while disruptions to flights connecting Bangladesh with Saudi Arabia have affected 5,418 passengers.
For many expatriates, the consequences extend far beyond cancelled flights.
Workers stranded in Bangladesh fear losing their jobs and residency permits, while those already in Saudi Arabia report reduced wages, unemployment and growing uncertainty as regional tensions threaten business activity.
Saudi Arabia is home to more than 3.2 million Bangladeshis, many of whom work in relatively low-paid occupations, including construction, cleaning and domestic services.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam has warned that the conflict could seriously affect overseas employment and remittance inflows, while migration experts say Bangladesh’s longstanding dependence on Middle Eastern labour markets has left workers particularly vulnerable.
Flight disruptions have left thousands of Bangladeshi passengers uncertain about when they can travel to Saudi Arabia.
According to aviation authorities, 5,418 passengers have been affected by disruptions to flights connecting Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia.
Twelve direct Riyadh-bound flights have been cancelled, including four operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, three by Saudia and three by Riyadh Air.
Biman’s Saudi-bound flight cancellations have been reported through October 17, while US-Bangla Airlines has announced the suspension of its Dhaka-Riyadh-Dhaka services until October 21.
For workers returning after leave, these delays could threaten their employment.
Jamal Uddin, stranded at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, said his employer had warned him of serious consequences if he failed to return on time.
“My leave ends on the 15th; the company warned that if I don’t report for duty on time, they will mark me absent and cancel my Iqama,” he said, referring to his Saudi residency permit.
“Now there are no flights, and I fear losing my job.”
Many workers face similar problems, particularly those whose visas or residency arrangements are approaching expiry.
The government has announced plans to arrange alternative flights through operational Saudi airports for passengers facing urgent visa or employment deadlines.
State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism M Rashiduzzaman Millat said on Monday that arrangements were being made to help stranded expatriates return to their workplaces.
For Bangladeshis already in Saudi Arabia, the difficulties began well before the latest security crisis.
Jamal Hossain, from Comilla, works for a cleaning company in Al-Kharj, near Riyadh.
He said his monthly salary had been cut in half after his employer cited a shortage of work.
“I joined this new company seven months ago. Things were fine for the first three months, but now they claim there is less work. Instead of 1,400 riyals, they are paying 700,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
Jamal said he had borrowed Tk350,000 to migrate to Saudi Arabia and was now struggling to meet his financial obligations.
He also complained about the increased cost of the Takamul skills verification examination, saying the fee had risen from $50 to $85 and that workers were bearing the additional expense.
His experience reflects wider concerns about wage irregularities and the vulnerability of low-paid migrant workers.
Human Rights Watch reported last November that at least 600 migrant workers from Bangladesh, India and Pakistan had gone unpaid for more than eight months.
Some affected workers also reported difficulties renewing their residency permits, leaving them unable to change jobs or return home easily.
For some newly arrived migrants, securing a Saudi visa has not translated into employment.
Sohel Rana, from Chittagong, travelled to Riyadh two months ago through a manpower supply company.
He said the recruiting agent had promised him direct employment, but the reality was very different.
“Upon arrival, I found fourteen people sharing a single room. Every morning, I stand at the labour market; if I get work, I earn 50 riyals, but otherwise, I return empty-handed.”
Last month, he said, he found work on only nine days.
Workers employed through supply agencies appear particularly vulnerable when construction and other projects slow down.
Rafiqul, a Bangladeshi worker from Shariatpur employed in Dammam, said his company had decided to send workers home after they demanded higher wages.
“Our company has decided to send us back home. We had demanded a pay raise, but they say our contract has ended,” he said.
His residency permit had also expired, leaving him fearful of detention.
“If the police catch me, I’ll end up in jail,” he said.
These accounts highlight the risks faced by migrants who have spent substantial sums securing overseas employment but find themselves without regular work or valid residency documents.
The latest escalation has added a direct threat to workers’ safety.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people, including two Bangladeshis, and injured 309 others, according to figures cited in the draft.
Another 24 Bangladeshis were injured, including 11 workers and 13 Umrah pilgrims.
Three were reported to be receiving treatment in intensive care at King Abdullah Hospital, with their conditions described as stable.
The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh has been coordinating with Saudi authorities to monitor the injured and assist affected nationals.
The attack, blamed on Houthi rebels, has heightened concerns over the safety of civilians and critical infrastructure in the kingdom.
It has also disrupted aviation services, creating additional problems for workers whose employment depends on timely travel between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia.
The impact is being felt beyond wage earners.
Nurul Afsar, a businessman from Feni who operates an electronics business in Jeddah, said the security situation was discouraging customers.
“I haven’t yet been able to recover from the losses caused by the coronavirus. Now, customers are afraid to visit. The shop remains empty after sunset,” he said.
“We business owners are facing extreme uncertainty.”
Workers also reported that some companies were suspending projects or reducing operations, citing the conflict.
Those dependent on daily wages and short-term assignments are among the most exposed because they have little financial protection when work stops.
Saudi Arabia remains Bangladesh’s largest overseas employment destination, despite longstanding concerns about low wages, recruitment costs and the quality of jobs available to migrants.
According to the draft’s labour migration figures, overseas employment clearances in September fell by approximately 29% compared with the same month last year.
The decline comes amid instability in the Middle East, restrictions in other traditional labour markets and limited progress in developing alternative destinations.
State Minister Shama Obaid Islam said some Bangladeshi expatriates had already lost their jobs and returned home, while others remained abroad without employment.
She warned that prolonged instability could affect both overseas employment and remittances.
The government was exploring new labour markets and promoting skilled, legal migration to reduce Bangladesh’s dependence on traditional destinations, she said.
Shariful Hasan, associate director at Brac, said the current crisis exposed a longstanding structural weakness in Bangladesh’s labour migration strategy.
“For the past decade and a half, there have been repeated calls to avoid centring our labour market solely on the Middle East and to seek alternative markets; we are now witnessing the consequences of that,” he said.
He warned that even if the conflict ended, its economic effects could persist.
The Middle East had attracted substantial international investment because it was regarded as relatively secure, he said. The latest conflict could undermine that confidence, affecting construction, tourism, hospitality and other industries that employ large numbers of migrants.
As businesses reduce investment and operations, workers could face fewer jobs, lower wages and further layoffs, he cautioned.
Against the deteriorating security situation, the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh has urged expatriates to remain vigilant, avoid high-risk and crowded areas, and follow Saudi authorities’ instructions.
In an advisory issued on Sunday, the embassy warned Bangladeshis against recording or sharing photographs, videos and sensitive information related to the conflict, citing restrictions under Saudi law.
The mission also provided emergency contact numbers for workers and other expatriates requiring assistance.
The embassy can be contacted on 8001000125 for labour-related matters, 8001000126 for passport services and 8001000124 for diplomatic assistance. For emergencies involving deaths, it provided +966570212180.
For millions of Bangladeshi families dependent on earnings from Saudi Arabia, the immediate concern is whether workers can remain safe and employed.

item.title: Saudi Arabia vows retaliation as strikes spread
item.description:
Saudi Arabia’s energy minister on Monday said the country had been tested but would mount a “serious” response after a string of attacks on Riyadh’s international airport by Yemen’s Houthis that left 18 people dead.
Lethal airport strikes since last week have rocked the world’s top oil exporter, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.
Yemen’s civil war, where a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis, has reignited months into the US-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
“Energy security can’t be taken for granted,” Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh, as oil prices topped $105 a barrel.
“The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious.”
“For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience,” he added.
On Saturday, Houthi strikes killed 13 people and wounded hundreds at King Khalid International Airport -- the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
Four people died in earlier attacks on Wednesday and Thursday, and another was killed on Sunday. Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh’s outskirts on Monday.
CCTV footage of Saturday’s attack released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Monday, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats, and Australia’s embassy warned its citizens in the city to shelter in place.
The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the previous 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting Saudi transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces.”
Hours later, the coalition said yet another projectile had struck Riyadh airport, sparking a fire, while air defenses intercepted a missile nearby.
AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the capital on Sunday.
“The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighborhood in the city’s north.
Riyadh’s airport was not the only one to suffer a deadly attack: early on Monday, officials said one person had been killed and 11 wounded in a strike on Dammam airport.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.
Riyadh hosts a packed calendar of events at this time of year, including its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, which draws foreign leaders and business titans.
Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defenses.
“Saudi air defenses have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively.”
The attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was “deeply concerned” over the recent escalation.
Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath.
“Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them.”

item.title: Shama: Middle East conflict may hit remittance inflows; new markets being explored
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Monday acknowledged that the conflict could have an immediate impact on remittances as many Bangladeshi workers in the Middle East have lost their jobs, while some have been forced to return home and others are struggling to remain in the region without employment.
Such disruptions could affect remittance inflows, she said, noting that Saudi Arabia alone hosts more than three million Bangladeshis.
Responding to a question after attending a seminar, Shama, however, expressed optimism that the government would be able to overcome the challenges in the long run by exploring new overseas employment markets.
The Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are working to identify new destinations for Bangladeshi workers.
The government also aims to create employment opportunities for those who have returned home after losing their jobs abroad, she added.
Shama said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has emphasized skilled migration and technical education to expand legal overseas employment and curb irregular migration.
She expressed hope that Bangladeshi workers would be able to access new job markets through improved skills and technical training.
Mentioning the recent attacks in Saudi Arabia, Shama said Bangladesh has lost two nationals in the incidents over the past two days, while at least 24 other Bangladeshis are receiving treatment at different hospitals in the country. Several of them are in intensive care units (ICUs), she said.
“We hope this situation will come to an end soon and the war will stop, as ordinary people are being killed and families are being destroyed,” the state minister said.
She said the government is closely monitoring the situation and hoped the conflict would end soon to prevent further casualties and suffering.
Asked about the possible impact of the conflict on Bangladesh's energy security, Shama said the government has long been working to achieve greater self-sufficiency in the energy sector by exploring alternative sources.
Under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the energy ministry has been working to identify new sources of energy, she said.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit is currently in Saudi Arabia to discuss energy cooperation between Bangladesh and the kingdom, Shama added.
She, however, said she has not received any indication of an immediate problem in the country's energy sector due to the conflict.
“This is not my department. You will get a better understanding if you speak to the energy minister,” the state minister said, expressing hope that the ministry's preparations and plans would help Bangladesh cope with any potential disruption.
If the war creates problems for Bangladesh, she said, the impact would not be confined to the country, as nations across the world could face similar difficulties. “We do not see ourselves in that situation at this moment,” she added.
Asked whether Bangladesh would send troops to Saudi Arabia if requested, Shama said Bangladesh has not yet joined the Mecca Pact.
“You can say that a decision has been taken only when it is formally announced. We have not joined the Mecca Pact yet, so the question of sending troops does not arise at this moment,” she said.
Shama said Bangladesh stood in solidarity with the Saudi government and people and wanted an immediate end to the attacks.
Responding to a question about the security of Mecca and Madinah, the state minister said the issue carried both diplomatic and emotional significance for Muslims around the world.
She said Bangladesh, where the majority of the population is Muslim, would not remain unmoved if the two holy cities faced a threat, adding that the country would extend a helping hand in such a situation.
The state minister said the increasingly complex international order, intensifying strategic rivalries and regional conflicts underscore the need for a foreign policy that responds to emerging realities while remaining firmly anchored in Bangladesh’s national interests.
“In this interconnected world, a crisis in one region has far-reaching and lasting consequences for others,” she said, noting that decisions taken in one capital can shape trade flows across continents, while geopolitical rivalries among major powers can influence the strategic choices available to countries far beyond their immediate neighborhood.
Speaking at the seminar, Shama said the evolving international landscape has made the discussion particularly timely.
Referring to the ongoing conflicts and growing instability around the world, the state minister said Bangladesh is also facing the consequences of the unfolding global turmoil.
“We are actually living in a global turmoil,” she said, highlighting the far-reaching implications of international conflicts.
She said Bangladesh needed a foreign policy that was not only responsive to emerging international realities but also guided by its national interests as the global landscape continued to evolve.
Shama also thanked the prime minister for holding a three-hour open discussion with over 200 members of parliament, allowing them to raise issues concerning their constituencies and the country as a whole.
She said the prime minister urged lawmakers to remain vigilant to ensure that the upcoming Durga Puja was celebrated peacefully across the country.
Given the sensitivity surrounding the festival, she said, lawmakers have been asked to work in their respective constituencies to maintain peace and communal harmony.
She alleged that elements associated with the previous fascist regime and other groups could attempt to disrupt the celebrations, stressing the need for vigilance to prevent any untoward incident.
On local government elections, Shama said there is no need for fresh instructions, adding that the ruling BNP would consider its position regarding candidates in union parishad elections and by-elections when those polls are held.
Asked about India, she said Bangladesh has no assessment to offer at the moment, describing the matter as an internal issue of India.
Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) organized the seminar titled “Foreign Policy of Bangladesh: Navigating Pathways in a Shifting World” at the BIISS auditorium.
BIISS Director General Major General A S M Ridwanur Rahman began the session with welcome remarks and chaired it.
Four papers were presented by BIISS researchers Dr Mahfuz Kabir, Research Director, Dr Sufia Khanom, Research Director, ASM Tarek Hassan Semul, Research Fellow, and Ayesha Binte Towhid, Research Fellow.
The speakers explored the importance of advancing a national interest-driven foreign policy responsive to emerging geopolitical realities while safeguarding national sovereignty and strategic autonomy.
Particular emphasis was placed on aligning foreign policy with contemporary defense and security priorities to address emerging challenges and preserve regional stability.
The program examined ways to prioritize Bangladesh’s economic interests within an increasingly uncertain multilateral system, notably amidst the rapid growth of AI, with a view to strengthening economic resilience and expanding international cooperation.
Significance of upholding ideological commitments and principled values in shaping a consistent credible foreign policy was underscored.
Discussions stressed on the need of building a balanced, pragmatic, and forward-looking foreign policy framework that would advance Bangladesh’s national interests while reinforcing its role as a responsible actor in the global arena.
Senior officials from different ministries of Bangladesh, foreign diplomatic missions, media, businesspeople, teachers and students from various universities, researchers, representatives from various think tanks were present.

item.title: Nearly 10,000 BGB members to be deployed for Durga Puja security
item.description:
Nearly 10,000 members of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) will be deployed nationwide from October 16 to 22 to ensure security during Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of the Hindu community.
Lieutenant Colonel Md Mahbub Murshed Rahman, director of operations at BGB headquarters, disclosed the deployment plan.
He said the BGB had adopted a comprehensive security plan to ensure peaceful and festive celebrations, focusing on regular patrols, intelligence surveillance and close coordination with local administrations, police and Puja celebration committees.
“The plan prioritises early identification of potential risks, vigilance against rumours and communal incitement, and a swift response to any untoward incidents,” he said.
The BGB will provide security assistance at 2,727 puja mandaps, including those within eight kilometres of the border and near battalion headquarters, he said.
Temporary camps will also be set up at strategic locations to ensure rapid patrols and assistance in remote and hard-to-reach areas.
In Dhaka, the scope of BGB deployment and its responsibilities will be determined based on government directives and requests from the relevant authorities, he said.
The force will coordinate with the Dhaka Metropolitan Police and local administration to conduct patrols, provide security at key locations and respond swiftly to emergencies as needed.
Describing Durga Puja as a reflection of Bangladesh’s longstanding tradition of communal harmony and mutual respect, Lieutenant Colonel Mahbub said the BGB was fully prepared to ensure that members of the Hindu community could celebrate the festival safely and joyfully.

item.title: UP elections to be held in five phases from Jan 21
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) has decided to hold the upcoming union parishad (UP) elections in five phases, with the first phase of voting scheduled for January 21 next year.
The election timeframe was finalized at a meeting of the Commission held at the Nirbachan Bhaban in the city's Agargaon area on Monday.
After the meeting, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah briefed reporters on the dates for the five phases of the elections.
According to the EC's decision, the second phase of voting will be held on February 4, the third phase on April 29, the fourth phase on May 13 and the fifth phase on May 27.
Sanaullah said around 4,300 union parishads have completed their five-year terms or would enter the election cycle within this period, making them eligible for elections under the law.
He said all five phases of voting would be held on Thursdays.
The district election officers will announce the election schedules for the respective union parishads, the election commissioner said.
"Generally, our district election officers will announce the schedules around six weeks before voting. The gap between the announcement of the schedule and polling may be around 38 to 45 days," he said.
Referring to the latest national election, Sanaullah said it was the most peaceful election in the country. "We hope to sustain the culture of good elections that we have started. All relevant stakeholders will extend their cooperation in this regard," he said.
On September 14, the EC announced a tentative schedule for the UP elections, initially planning to hold the polls in seven phases from November 12.
Earlier on September 14, the Election Commission first announced the possible timeframe for the staggered UP election starting on November 12 this year. However, the relevant ministries and departments in a meeting with the EC on September 17 suggested not starting the local body elections in November and December as public examinations would be held in schools at the time.

item.title: Three years after October 7, global attention on Gaza has receded. The real test will come after Israel’s election
item.description:
This week marks three years since Hamas’ massacre of October 7 , 2023, in which some 1,200 people, most of them Israeli civilians, were killed and 251 taken hostage.
What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry , leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.
A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides -- though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank .
Despite this, global attention on Gaza has waned. As the US–Israeli war with Iran began dominating the headlines, earlier pledges by many states to help drive the peace process forward have proved once again wanting, even hollow.
Now, Israel is preparing for a highly polarized parliamentary election on October 27, which could be consequential for the entire region. If a less extreme government takes office, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank -- and the pressure it has generated -- hold?
What the peace plan delivered, and what it didn’t
The first phase of US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan in Gaza largely succeeded. The remaining living Israeli hostages came home in exchange for close to 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees , and the remains of deceased hostages were returned over the following months. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Gazans moved back to the north. Israeli forces pulled back to a “yellow line”, and the UN Security Council endorsed the plan and a US-chaired “Board of Peace”.
However, the world’s expectations for “all guns to fall silent” were soon dashed. A year after the ceasefire was signed on October 9 , 2025, the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures the UN uses, reports close to 1,400 Gazans have been killed.
Aid remains restricted, meaningful reconstruction has yet to begin, and another winter is approaching for families living in tents and damaged buildings.
Without sustained international engagement, the second phase of the Trump plan has largely stalled. Hamas has not disarmed. An International Stabilization Force intended to bring security to Gaza has yet to deploy , despite a US commander being appointed in January. And the technocratic Palestinian committee meant to run Gaza has not taken control on the ground.
Only last week did the Board of Peace unveil a six-month, US$2.45 billion plan to begin rebuilding, but this is a fraction of the US$71.4 billion it estimates recovery will require over a decade.
And all of this depends on Hamas surrendering its weapons. Israel will not allow reconstruction before full disarmament, and Hamas will not disarm on the plan’s terms. Reform of the domestically unpopular Palestinian Authority has been slow, and Israel’s right-wing government has been in campaign mode for months, with strong incentives to spoil the progress.
Recognition of Palestine by more than 150 states has not changed the reality on the ground. The international pressure that helped bring about the ceasefire has proved much harder to sustain since the worst of the violence ended.
Attention faded, but did not disappear
Media and public attention to distant atrocities is notoriously short-lived. It peaks with the most extreme violence and quickly subsides once violence becomes chronic, or once another crisis begins to dominate the news.
Gaza has followed part of this script. As mass casualty bombardments gave way to near-daily “lower-intensity” attacks, headlines receded . The US–Israeli war with Iran, which began in late February, absorbed much of the world’s limited attention span . Ukraine and, in short bursts, Lebanon, competed for what remained.
Most people rank foreign crises far below domestic concerns – health care, jobs and the cost of living -- and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reached directly into people’s pockets through the price of petrol. Gaza, for most, never did.
A year ago, I warned that once the mass violence in Gaza ended, international attention would wane, making it easier for either side to derail the peace process. That is largely what happened, but not entirely.
What stands out about the past year is less the weakening of attention to Gaza than the extent to which some of it remained. While mass opinion largely moved on, elite opinion (some legislators, officials, commentators) and the smaller but highly committed body of concerned global citizens did not.
The latter drew on a Palestinian solidarity movement built over decades, turning outrage into a sustained global campaign -- though some of their rhetoric and tactics also deepened polarization , at home and in Israel.
Sudan, meanwhile, which the UN has described as the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, shows the flip side . With no equivalent global campaign behind it, it has struggled to hold the world’s gaze.
The invisibility of one crisis and the hyper-visibility of another are two faces of the same problem: which atrocities galvanise public opinion depends less on their severity than on who is organised enough to make us pay attention.
A deepening crisis in the West Bank
The sustained, if narrower, global pressure campaign on Gaza soon had a new source of outrage: settler violence in the West Bank.
The United Nations had recorded an average of six settler attacks on Palestinians a day by June of this year, a pace higher than any year on record. By July , killings linked to settler attacks had exceeded the total for all of 2025. Thousands of Palestinians have also been displaced as settlement expansion has accelerated.
Some European governments had already banned trade with the settlements ; others, such as the United Kingdom, more recently found they could no longer afford to ignore the crisis. In September, London announced its ban , with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accusing “settler terrorists” of ethnic cleansing.
Although the European Union is Israel’s largest trading partner and the UK another important one, the economic impact of these measures will be modest since settlements export relatively little. The significance is mainly political.
Moreover, if the European pressure is meant in part to sway Israeli voters before the election, it’s unclear how effective it will be. Outside pressure before an election tends to rally a leader’s loyal base, and the global outrage over Gaza has already reinforced a siege mentality among many Israeli Jews.
The real external pressure, however, will need to come after the election.
The decisive stick for moving the peace process forward lies in Washington, given how much any Israeli government depends on US support. The main carrot for Israel would be normalization of relations with Saudi Arabia – and with it much of the Arab and Muslim world. But this is a reward Riyadh has tied to a credible path to Palestinian statehood.
Another factor will weigh even more, and it is often underestimated: the Israeli public’s profound need for a sense of security .
Shattered on October 7, this need helps explain how the war in Gaza was fought, though it cannot excuse it -- just as no grievance, whatever its roots, could justify Hamas’ massacre of civilians.
It will now shape how Israelis vote -- and what any new government believes it can risk -- far more than sticks or carrots from abroad.
The harder test: shades of grey
Last year, I argued that meaningful progress in Gaza and the West Bank would require an Israeli government willing to make hard choices.
The October 27 election will be a test of whether one emerges. Polls suggest Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar could become the largest party in the Knesset (Israel’s parliament), but it may struggle to form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, a prospect Eisenkot has refused to embrace.
A change of government would matter. It could bring a real effort to rein in settler violence, a more cooperative approach to the Board of Peace’s efforts in Gaza, and a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks.
However, it is less likely to bring a fundamental change in policy on Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories. Eisenkot has ruled out a Palestinian state for the foreseeable future , and any coalition he leads would probably include right-wing partners.
Herein lies a paradox. Global action is most easily mobilised against clearly villainous actions and actors. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition, including far-right ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, has made the case for international pressure easy.
A more moderate-sounding, centre -right government would make it much harder to sustain. Governments that could not ignore Israel’s conduct under Netanyahu may ease off their pressure. Some media may treat an Eisenkot-led victory as a path towards resolution, and concerned citizens may struggle to keep people’s attention focused on an occupation that grinds on more quietly.
If sustained attention depends on extreme cases, then the quieter periods in between are where policies stall and abuses continue. The past year suggests that outrage alone cannot carry meaningful pressure through those periods.
Three years after October 7, the guns in Gaza are quieter, but far from silent. The question for the year ahead is whether the world keeps listening.
Eyal Mayroz is Senior Lecturer in Peace and Conflict Studies, University of Sydne y. This article previously appeared in the Conversation and has been reprinted under special arrangement.

item.title: Nepal rescuers search for missing after flash flood
item.description:
Nepali rescuers searched for five missing people on Monday, a day after devastating flash floods swept away more than 200 houses and five bridges along the Budhi Gandaki river.
Videos showed a dark, debris-filled river surging through the hills in central Nepal’s Gorkha district.
No deaths have been confirmed.
On Sunday, 95 people including nine foreigners were rescued.
“We are continuing our work on rescue and relief,” Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal Army spokesman told AFP, adding that four helicopters had been deployed.
“We do not have any new information on the five missing,” he added.
About 150 foreign trekkers are in the area, according to the Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal, many on the popular Manaslu circuit trek.
“We are working with authorities to rescue those who are stranded because of the roads,” the association’s president Sagar Pandey said.
Authorities were also delivering aid to affected communities, with many residents fleeing their homes on Sunday morning as the torrent hit.
The flood also struck hydropower plants, according to the national disaster agency.
“I screamed out loud to get people out. Just a few minutes after people ran out the flood crashed through,” local resident Indra Bahadur Gurung said.
“We have always lived here, and find it difficult to leave. I hope the government will manage something safe for us soon.”
Preliminary data suggests that a landslide had dammed the river. It then burst, with the water surging downstream.
“The government has already begun taking the necessary steps to restore normal life,” Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a post on social media late Sunday.
He urged residents to stay in safe locations and to avoid travel on risky roads and bridges.
Nepal is still recovering from devastating floods on August 26, triggered by a mountain glacial collapse, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.
Shah told the United Nations last month that the August flooding “was a warning to the world” about the rising dangers of climate change.
Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University, said that the latest flood showed the need for better monitoring.
“The frequency of the disasters is dangerous... it shows we need to go beyond our traditional river-level based early warning systems,” Adhikari said, suggesting satellite images and seismometers could help detect events earlier.
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said Sunday that the floods highlighted the “range of hazards capable of generating destructive floods” in Himalayan river systems.
“Understanding what triggered this flood will be critical for reducing future risks and strengthening resilience,” the centre’s director general Pema Gyamtsho said in the statement.
Heavy rainfall in late September also triggered floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the disaster agency.

item.title: Americans Hall and Woodford win economics Nobel for stabilization models
item.description:
Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can better stabilize disruptive economic fluctuations.
The two were honored for developing new models for managing recessions and other crises that fail to respond to traditional tools.
“On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the jury said.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained in a statement that ever since John Maynard Keynes formulated his economic theories almost a century ago, “stabilization” policies had long let officials boost economic growth when needed.
But during the oil shocks in the 1970s, the Keynesian models that governed when and how action should be taken no longer worked.
Hall, 83, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University born in 1955, separately began to explore new models.
“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the jury said.
Hall and Woodford’s models include an “understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions,” it said.
A fundamental aspect of this is the understanding that households are forward-looking when making decisions about spending or saving.
This means the way governments and central banks communicate their policies can influence people’s views of the future when making such decisions.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
“It’s a surprise, but I’m feeling very good about it,” Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt “elated” for receiving “a tremendous honor.”
While his theories have had a large impact on policymakers, he said they had not been “motivated by a specific political agenda.”
“It was an attempt to improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy and therefore to contribute both to the management of the economy, but also to contribute to public understanding,” Woodford said.
The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.
It was instead created through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968.
But like the Nobels in chemistry and physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.
Last year, the economics award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.
Last week, South African judge Navi Pillay won the peace prize, and Canadian-Icelandic writer Anne Carson was named the literature laureate.
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Frenchman Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai of Japan, and the Physics Prize to Belgian Francis Halzen.
And the first prize to be announced, in medicine, went to American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.
The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.

item.title: Pakistan detains hundreds from ex-PM Khan’s party in northern province
item.description:
Pakistani authorities have detained hundreds of members of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party after emergency rule was imposed in a northern province, police officials told AFP on Monday.
Two police officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media, said 278 members of Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party had been detained in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province since Sunday’s emergency declaration.
The PTI-ruled province was placed under emergency rule following days-long anti-government protests demanding Khan’s release, while militant violence in the area has also been mounting, particularly along the border with Afghanistan.
Thousands of Khan’s supporters have been marching in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, also airing anti-government grievances fueled by harsh economic conditions.
The hugely popular former cricket star’s party said on Sunday the province’s chief minister Sohail Afridi had been arrested hours after the extraordinary constitutional measures were announced by Pakistan’s presidency.
An administrative official, also speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Afridi had been placed in “protective custody” in his official residence but later moved to another location.
The official declined to disclose the new location.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is a stronghold for Khan’s party, and the PTI-led government there would be “non-functional” until the security situation improves, the government said.
Islamabad has accused the PTI administration in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa of failing to deal with the militants, necessitating the imposition of emergency rule.
The PTI has vehemently opposed the constitutional measures, describing them as undemocratic and a grab for power by the federal government.
Khan has been behind bars since August 2023, facing scores of charges ranging from corruption to inciting violence, following widespread anti-establishment riots in May that year.
He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated.

item.title: BADC marks 65 years with focus on food security
item.description:
Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC), which marks its 65th anniversary on 16 October, is expanding its role in seed production, irrigation, fertiliser distribution and agricultural technology as Bangladesh seeks to strengthen food security and modernise farming.
Established on October 16, 1961, the state-run corporation produced 144,000 tonnes of seeds and distributed 147,000 tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year, said a press release.
BADC began distributing seeds in 1962-63 with around 13.8 tonnes. It now supplies seeds for rice, wheat, maize, potatoes, jute, pulses, spices, vegetables and oilseeds, working with 105,775 contract farmers.
Its research cell has registered 40 high-yielding and promising crop varieties. The corporation is also prioritising varieties tolerant of salinity, drought and waterlogging to help farmers adapt to climate change.
During FY26, BADC projects extended irrigation facilities to an additional 22,000 hectares. The
corporation excavated or re-excavated 820 kilometres of canals, constructed 662 irrigation structures and installed 161 solar-powered irrigation pumps.
Under a government five-year plan to restore 20,000 kilometres of canals and waterways nationwide, BADC has been assigned 9,000 kilometres of work to improve surface-water availability and expand irrigation.
The corporation imported 2.627 million tonnes of non-urea fertiliser in FY26 and distributed 2.401 million tonnes, meeting 75.37% of national demand. It supplies subsidised fertiliser through 148 warehouses across 64 districts.
BADC has also proposed converting 50,900 diesel-powered irrigation pumps to solar power across 56 districts. The project is expected to save Tk176.40 crore annually.
To reduce dependence on imported seeds, the corporation aims to produce 5,000 tonnes of jute seeds annually from the 2029-30 production year. It is also expanding domestic hybrid maize and summer onion seed production.
Meanwhile, BADC has established 82 polytunnels nationwide, with another 60 planned by June 2028, to support year-round cultivation. Its fresh-produce treatment facility in Gabtali, Dhaka, has also begun treating mangoes for domestic consumption and export.
BADC Chairman Md Azizul Islam has stressed responsible and transparent service delivery to advance agricultural development and strengthen national food security.
